---
title: "Chapter 7: Zep Tepi - The First Time"
---

## The First Time

The Egyptians called it **Zep Tepi**—"the First Time" or "the First Occasion."

Zep Tepi was the primordial age when the gods walked the earth, when the principles of cosmic order were established, when the patterns that governed all subsequent existence were laid down. It was not merely the beginning of history but the template for history—the original performance of which all later events were echoes and repetitions.

The Pyramid Texts, inscribed on the walls of Old Kingdom tombs and representing the oldest religious literature on earth, refer repeatedly to Zep Tepi. The gods acted; the world came into being; the patterns were set. Everything that came after—every ritual, every temple, every pharaoh—was a re-enactment of Zep Tepi, an attempt to maintain the original order against the forces of chaos.

Who ruled during Zep Tepi? The ancient king-lists are explicit: the gods themselves. Before the dynasties of human pharaohs, before even the semi-divine "followers of Horus," the gods held kingship.

The Turin Royal Canon, a papyrus from around 1300 BCE, lists the reigns of divine pharaohs extending back tens of thousands of years before the first human dynasty. The historian Manetho, writing in the 3rd century BCE, describes a period of 24,925 years during which the gods, and then the "spirits of the dead," ruled Egypt.

24,925 years. The precessional cycle is 25,920 years. The difference is less than 4%.

---

## What the Gods Taught

According to Egyptian tradition, the god Thoth—called Djehuti in Egyptian—invented writing, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and magic. He was the ibis-headed god of wisdom, the scribe of the gods, the keeper of the celestial archives.

Thoth was not a distant creator. He was a teacher. The texts attributed to him—collected in what later Greeks would call the "Hermetic" corpus after identifying Thoth with their own Hermes—contained the accumulated wisdom of divine civilization.

The "42 Books of Thoth" allegedly contained everything: cosmology and theology, astronomy and astrology, medicine and magic, ritual and hymn. These books were kept in temple libraries, accessible only to initiated priests who had proven their worthiness and their discretion.

Whether the 42 Books literally existed as a fixed collection or represent a conceptual category for "all sacred knowledge," the claim is clear: Egyptian wisdom was not invented by Egyptians. It was inherited from the gods. It was taught during Zep Tepi. It was preserved, not created.

---

## The Edfu Building Texts

On the walls of the Temple of Horus at Edfu—completed in 57 BCE but built on the site of much older structures—are inscribed texts that describe the mythological origins of Egyptian temples.

According to these texts, the first temples were built not by humans but by a group called the Shebtiw—"the founders" or "the ancestors." These beings arrived in Egypt after a great catastrophe had destroyed their original homeland, referred to as "the Island of the Egg" or "the Homeland of the Primeval Ones."

The Shebtiw brought with them knowledge of temple construction, of sacred architecture, of the rituals that maintained cosmic order. They established "sacred mounds" at locations that would later become the great temple sites of Egypt. They laid down the patterns that all subsequent temples would follow.

The Edfu texts describe these founders in language remarkably similar to the Mesopotamian accounts of the Apkallu: beings who came from elsewhere (across water), who survived a catastrophe (that destroyed their homeland), who brought the arts of civilization (temple-building, ritual, knowledge), and who established the foundations upon which later culture would build.

The parallel may not be coincidental. Both traditions may be encoding the same memory.

---

## The Followers of Horus

Between the reign of the gods and the first human dynasty, Egyptian tradition places an intermediate period ruled by the **Shemsu-Hor**—the "Followers of Horus."

These were semi-divine beings, not quite gods but more than human. They maintained the traditions established during Zep Tepi and transmitted them to the first human pharaohs. They were the link between the divine age and the historical age.

The Palermo Stone, an Old Kingdom document listing the reigns of early pharaohs, refers to the Shemsu-Hor as a distinct category of pre-dynastic rulers. The Turin Canon assigns them a reign of 13,420 years.

Again, the numbers are striking. 13,420 is just over half a precessional cycle (25,920 ÷ 2 = 12,960). The Egyptians appear to be encoding astronomical time-scales in their accounts of mythological history.

Who were the Shemsu-Hor? The orthodox interpretation is that they were legendary or mythological figures with no historical reality. The alternative interpretation is that they represent a real priesthood or ruling class that preserved pre-catastrophe knowledge through the dark age that followed the Younger Dryas.

Either way, their function in the tradition is clear: to transmit. To carry knowledge from the age of the gods to the age of men. To ensure that Zep Tepi was not forgotten.

---

## Continuity and Conservation

What distinguishes Egyptian civilization is its conservatism. Where other cultures innovated, adapted, and transformed, Egypt preserved.

The temples built in the Ptolemaic period (332–30 BCE) follow the same architectural principles as temples built two thousand years earlier. The rituals performed in them were recognizable evolutions of Old Kingdom practices. The hieroglyphic script, though it accumulated additional signs, remained fundamentally the same from its earliest appearances until the last temple closures in the 4th century CE.

This conservatism was not accidental. It was ideological. The Egyptians believed that the patterns established during Zep Tepi were perfect—that any deviation from them was a falling away from original perfection. The goal was not progress but preservation, not innovation but restoration.

The pharaoh's role was explicitly to maintain Ma'at—cosmic order—against the forces of Isfet—chaos. Every temple ritual, every festival, every offering was a renewal of the original pattern, a re-creation of Zep Tepi that kept the world functioning.

This meant that knowledge from Zep Tepi was not merely respected but actively preserved. Changes were resisted. Innovations were disguised as restorations. The claim was always that current practice reflected original truth.

If any culture would successfully transmit pre-catastrophe knowledge across millennia, it would be Egypt.

---

## The Question of Origins

When did Egyptian civilization begin?

The orthodox answer is approximately 3100 BCE, with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under the first pharaoh (traditionally called Menes or Narmer). Before this, there was a "pre-dynastic" period of gradual development, with the emergence of agriculture, pottery, and social complexity following the patterns seen elsewhere in the Neolithic.

But this answer is complicated by several anomalies.

**The Sphinx**: The Great Sphinx of Giza shows weathering patterns that some geologists interpret as water erosion—patterns that would require extended periods of rainfall. Egypt has not had such rainfall since before 5000 BCE, and some estimates push the required rainfall back to before 7000 BCE. If this interpretation is correct, the Sphinx is far older than orthodox Egyptology allows.

**The Pyramid Texts**: The language and concepts in the Pyramid Texts (first inscribed around 2400 BCE) appear to be extremely old, preserving archaic features that suggest they were composed—or at least their core material was composed—long before they were written down. Some passages may represent oral traditions extending back to the Neolithic or earlier.

**The Astronomical Alignments**: The Giza pyramids and other Old Kingdom structures are aligned with remarkable precision to cardinal directions and, some researchers argue, to stellar positions that would have been accurate not in 2500 BCE but in earlier millennia. Whether these alignments are intentional and what they might encode remains debated.

The Egyptians themselves claimed that their civilization was much older than modern archaeology admits. They claimed to preserve knowledge from Zep Tepi—from "the First Time." They may have been telling the truth.

## The Two Lands

Egypt was always conceived as a duality: Upper Egypt (the southern Nile Valley) and Lower Egypt (the northern Delta). The pharaoh wore the Double Crown, combining the red crown of Lower Egypt and the white crown of Upper Egypt. The kingdom was called "the Two Lands."

This duality was fundamental to Egyptian thought. Not opposition—like the Zoroastrian good versus evil—but complementarity. The Two Lands needed each other. Their union was the basis of order.

The same principle extended to cosmology. The world was divided into Duat (the underworld) and the sky, into the seen and the unseen, into the manifest and the unmanifest. The sun god Ra traveled through the Duat each night to be reborn each morning. Death was not ending but transition. The visible was sustained by the invisible.

This cosmological dualism has parallels in the framework we are tracing: the distinction between the manifest states (+1, -1) and the unmanifest void (0), the flux field that underlies manifestation, the threshold between potential and actual. Egypt may have intuited, and encoded, a structure that modern physics is now formalizing.

---

## Key Points

- Zep Tepi ("the First Time") was the Egyptian primordial age when gods walked the earth and established cosmic patterns
- The Turin Royal Canon assigns ~25,000 years to divine rule—closely matching the precessional cycle
- Thoth (Djehuti) was credited with inventing writing, mathematics, astronomy, and magic
- The Edfu texts describe founders (Shebtiw) who arrived after a catastrophe, paralleling the Apkallu tradition
- The Shemsu-Hor ("Followers of Horus") were semi-divine intermediaries who transmitted knowledge to human pharaohs
- Egyptian civilization was explicitly conservative, aiming to preserve Zep Tepi patterns rather than innovate
- Anomalies (Sphinx weathering, archaic Pyramid Texts, astronomical alignments) suggest possible deep antiquity
- Egyptian dualism (Two Lands, Duat/sky, seen/unseen) may encode fundamental metaphysical structure
